What this supports

No automatic deletion recommendation follows from this experiment. A greedy core preserves the observed requirements in the recorded matrix. It has not been established as a safe replacement for the full suite.

Shared responsibility

Select tests to simulate their joint removal against the fixed baseline requirements. This makes the risk of deleting an entire redundant group visible.

Observed kill matrix

Mutations target the same changed source files selected from the known fix. This is a retrospective comparison near known fault locations, not evidence of prospective whole-repository ranking. Each accepted replay must pass at the fixed revision, fail an assertion after the changed source is reverted to the parent, pass after restoration, and retain an unaffected test as a negative control. Every replay uses the fixed-revision test pool and the dependency installation recorded for its profile.

The ranking comparison simulates equal-size test selections from recorded per-test outcomes. It does not rerun selected subsets. Shared state or order effects could change actual subset behavior. The original historical profile selected fixes that change or add a selected test file. The expanded frozen cohort uses a separate adapted installation matched to each fix revision's declared lockfile and inputs. The handoff separates candidate counts, baseline-only validation and completed fault replays. Tests come from the fixed revision, so this evaluates retrospective fault sensitivity and does not validate usefulness before the fix.

Random seeds are repeated selections within a fault. The summary averages within each fault first, then across faults. The uncertainty interval resamples related-fault groups. This is a selected retrospective cohort. These intervals do not establish ranking superiority or performance on future faults.

Decisions

The prototype uses Archguard's mutation planner for TypeScript and cargo-mutants 27.1.0 for the optional Rust slice. The central calculation groups equal nonempty kill signatures and keeps those with no strictly smaller observed signature. The requirements remain fixed while tests are removed.

Each run gets a fresh owned source copy and private home, temporary and cache directories. External dependency bytes are copied and hashed, and workspace imports are rebuilt into that run's source. The runner rejects missing tests, retries, newly skipped tests, runtime failures, hook errors and unfinished publication.

The disk guard stops work at 12% free space, ahead of the user's 10% boundary. Process cleanup retains ownership of the leader until its group is settled. Uncertain cleanup preserves source copies and is recorded as incomplete.

Limits that matter

  • Dynamic subsumption depends on the available tests and sampled operators.
  • Surviving mutants may be equivalent, uncovered or insufficiently asserted. No equivalence proof was attempted.
  • Runtime is measured inside individual tests. Shared setup, compilation and runner startup remain separate.
  • Repeated passing baselines give observations of stability, not proof of zero flakiness. Maintenance cost was not measured.
  • The original profile uses copied modern dependency installations. The expanded profile matches declared installation inputs but disables lifecycle scripts and package-manager hooks. Both remain adapted reproductions; whole historical revision fidelity has not been established.
  • Fix-revision tests may include regressions written after the fault was understood. Matching parent test identities does not prove unchanged test bodies.
  • Selected mutation prefixes and test slices do not establish whole-repository effectiveness.

Scientific basis

Papadakis et al., ICSE 2018 motivates equal-size test comparisons and caution about mutation/fault correlations. Papadakis et al., ISSTA 2016 motivates removing redundant mutation requirements. Dynamic mutant subsumption using LittleDarwin describes the test-dependent kill-set relation.

The handoff's ASSENT paper is a useful methodological reference. Its publisher full text was unavailable during this run, so this report does not claim independent verification of its reported effect sizes.

A possible attribution follow-up

For the specific game that counts fixed requirements detected by any selected test, exact Shapley credit is simple: give each test 1/k for every requirement it kills, where k tests kill that requirement. A test is first among those k tests in one out of k random orderings. Sum those shares. This avoids exponential enumeration for this additive coverage game. It allocates observed capability; it is not a validated test-retention score, and this prototype does not rank tests by it.

Reproduce and continue

Next, verify actual selected-subset behavior, classify changed test bodies, enlarge independent fault groups, and compare operator budgets. Treat a retention/cost view as the product candidate. A single weighted quality score is not justified by these results.

Research proxy only. These measurements describe the recorded tests and mutants. They do not authorize deleting tests.
